summary: Broad-leaved pepperweed, also called tall pepperweed or perennial peppergrass, is a plant up to 5 feet tall with many stiff stems, waxy green leaves and dense clusters of tiny white flowers; it smells like horseradish. It forms large stands that crowd out native plants and reduce habitat for native birds, insects and other animals. In the Northeast it mainly invades salt marshes, competing with native marsh grasses, and sometimes grows along salted roads.
history: Broad-leaved pepperweed is native to southern Europe and western Asia, and may have been brought to the United States by accident in shipments of sugar beet seed. In the East it is found mainly along the coasts of New York and New England.
seasons: A rosette of leaves grows from late fall to early spring, and the plant flowers from late spring through summer and into fall. Old stems stay standing through the winter.

handling.text: Pulling or digging it out is not recommended because of its extensive roots, but mowing repeatedly before it sets seed may help hold it back.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
